21256-travels-through-the-south-of-franc:
Lieutenant-Colonel Pinkney of the North American Native Rangers travelled through southern France in 1807 and 1808. His route, he says, was never performed before: along the banks of the Loire, the Isère, and the Garonne. He travelled with the French government's permission. His book appeared in London in 1809.

He sails from Baltimore to Liverpool, crosses to Calais, buys a Norman horse, and posts south through Boulogne. Markets, prices, cottages, dances on the green, and French domestic economy fill his chapters. An American officer's view of Napoleonic France, written for English readers curious about the enemy's country, is the book's special value.

Yuri Orlov, who died in 2020 at ninety-six, was both a serious physicist and a founder of the Soviet human rights movement. Svetlana Savranskaya and Tom Blanton compiled this memorial briefing book, number 724. Orlov founded the Moscow Helsinki Group, which monitored Soviet compliance with human rights promises.

He proposed glasnost, openness, almost fifteen years before Gorbachev made it policy. For that work he paid with prison and exile. The memorial builds on an earlier 2014 briefing book on Orlov, updated at his death. It preserves the record of a scientist who treated truth telling as a method, in physics and in politics alike.
